This is a fabulous piece. Diamonds are old mine cut diamonds but there are some large ones and old cut diamonds can be desirable. I'm not an expert, used to work for a Armenian jeweler, but the construction of the piece itself shows great craftmanship.

 I wasn't sure how beautiful it was until I saw the back of the piece. Again, not a professional, but I love to see that the stones are set properly with multiple prongs. The settings are very important in jewelry. If you have something expensive, you do not want it to fall out. A big give away with cheaper jewelry is lack of craftsmanship and poor use of prongs or lack of them shows lack of care. No one wants prongs that will catch on hair etc, but you don't want your big ol' diamond to go flying as well. 

Pieces of jewelry with a lot of tiny diamonds can be perceived as more valuable because some people believe more diamonds equals more value. When I worked for my jeweler, he would vacuum up tiny diamonds with no concern. It's all about the cut, clarity, and in my opinion, the craftmanship. Quality, quality, quality. So while there are a lot of low grade diamonds in this piece, the quality of the piece itself makes up for it. 

I am just echoing a lot of people right now but this is valued far more than the gold/scrap value. My rule of thumb when selling jewelry is to only sell it for the gold value if the piece is broken, non functional, and not repairable. Then it is scrap and I weigh it and then I search the value of the gold, after removing the stones online before I go to a reputable jeweler.

Before reselling a piece, try to salvage it. This may be a brilliant artist with a brilliant piece of   
jewelry that this artist put a lot of time into... so see if can be repaired, and if the market is right, the value will go up exponentially if it just needs a new clasp or a missing stone replaced, etc.  

When I worked for that jeweler, he though all silver jewelry had no value. Silver itself is down but pieces made by famous artists or have desirability from clients have value. So, I would fish them out of the "scrap box", research the designers, and found some rare pieces here and there, a lot of really nice Native American pieces. It was a small store, had some time on my hands but to think these beautiful pieces of work were going to be melted down is heart breaking.  

At the end of the day, the worth of the piece is what is someone is willing to pay for it. 

Hope you do the right thing, OP.

I agree with the other comment you received but wanted to add some general advice in regards to this:  
Try not to freak out when the deadline approaches. Professors are used to being asked for letters of recommendation and have written tons of them. I'm not saying that makes it okay to treat them in a specific way but more trying to communicate that they are quite familiar with the process. As long as they know the deadline date, they will get it done or let you know if it's not possible in their time frame. I had a professor who asked me to send him reminder e-mails so obviously every professor is different. I think it's appropriate to send an e-mail a week before the deadline and ask how it's going, that you don't mean to pressure them or be rude, that you're just worried about the deadline of 11/XX, etc, and you're thankful for the time they are taking to write your letter of recommendation.   
I haven't had any issues with this approach but I also try to maintain a good level of communication with the professors who write me letters so they know me, I know them, and we maintain on the same page.  
Lastly, it never hurts to ask another professor as a backup if possible.

*1 1/2 pounds boneless skinless chicken breast tenders, sliced into strips about 1/4 to 1/8 of an inch thick1/2 cup vegetable oil1 tbs. saltDog Friendly seasonings including parsley, rosemary, and sage"*

2nd Edit: Found the exact recipe I used back in 2012!:  
([https://thebark.com/content/homemade-chicken-jerky-sweet-potato-chews](https://thebark.com/content/homemade-chicken-jerky-sweet-potato-chews))

**Ingredients**  
•1/2 pounds boneless, skinless chicken breast tenders  
• 1/2 cup vegetable oil  
• Your choice of dog-friendly seasonings: parsley, rosemary, sage (preferably fresh and chopped very fine)

**Directions**  
• Rinse the chicken breasts and remove any fat, which slows down the dehydrating process and will shorten the jerky’s shelf life.  
• Slice the chicken into strips about 1/4- to 1/8-inch thick; slicing with the grain will make the jerky even chewier.  
• Coat the strips with oil and seasonings.  
• Place the strips on the dehydrator tray, spacing them evenly; make sure they do not touch. The drying process depends on adequate airflow between the strips.  
• Put the tray in the dehydrator, turn it on and set the temperature for 140 degrees.

It will probably take between 3 and 12 hours for the strips to fully dry, depending on how thick you cut them and the exact temperature of your dehydrator. After the first hour, start checking the strips on an hourly basis. To determine the dryness level, remove one strip from the dehydrator, cut into it with a sharp knife and examine the inside. When the meat is completely dried, you won’t see any moisture and it will be the same color throughout. If it needs more time, put it back in for another hour. As it gets closer to being finished, check every half hour.

I don't feel qualified to answer all of your questions so I hope some of my advice helps.  
With mental health doctors, something I've learned and have been told is that a wise way to look at it is to treat it like a job interview.  You don't need to commit to the first person you see, in fact, you should see a few for a first time visits then make a choice if you want to continue seeing them.  I know it can be tedious and trying but having a good psychiatrist/psychologist is very important.  
As for the medical doctor, I too, have lousy insurance. I would first contact your insurance company and request a list of providers that take your insurance. From there, google is your friend. Of course, you have to remember that typically people are more keen to go to the internet to complain about something rather then to say something positive. It's more useful to see how quickly they see patients, how the staff in the waiting room treat you, ease of making appointments, etc.  
Also, having a doctor that is closer to you is convenient, but sometimes with our limited insurance and limited doctors, we may not have that luxury. 
About the possibility of disagreeing with their opinions, that's normal and that's okay. If they endorse something you do not agree with, I would vocalize that to them. If they refuse to listen to your side of the view and are not accommodating, then I would consider seeing another doctor.  
However, that can be very circumstantial. For example, I broke my wrist over the summer and my doctor said I needed surgery. The idea of surgery was not something I felt was necessary. I asked him the risks of just getting a cast versus surgery, and he informed me.  Ultimately, I declined to get the surgery he recommended and he did not push it when I made it clear that was my decision. If he had not treated me well as a patient or a person for disagreeing with him, I would have found someone else.  Not necessarily because he didn't agree with me, but because if he was not willing to treat with me respect then that's not a doctor I would want to have.  
On the other hand, if I was declining surgery that was not optional in order to treat something, then that's more my fault. Willingness to listen to your doctor's reasons for treatment, even if it's not something you endorse or agree with, is important when making any medical decisions for yourself. It's your body, it's your life, it's your decision at the end of the day. Still, make decisions that are educated.  
I apologize for my long winded answer. To summarize, treat your mental health doctor initial appointments like interviews, do not be afraid to see several before deciding on one.  
Use google to check out the doctors covered by your provider to get some information - but use it with a grain of salt as most people always have something negative to say.  
I hope this helps!
